title: Budget and cash flow
subtitle: The foundation of a good start
topics: Tell apart revenue, fixed costs and variable costs, both in your household budget and in your business (linked to the costs of your industry).
Understand liquidity: cash flow vs. "profit on paper".
Separate private money from business money at the start of the year.
challenge: Plan your monthly budget and get through the first month without a negative balance.

mission.title: Get through your first month with every bill paid

steps.label: Make sure every bill gets paid

mission.reward: Unlocks February and your first lesson

lessonCard.title: Cash keeps you alive
points: Revenue is not profit, and profit is not cash. A month can look profitable on paper and still leave you unable to pay rent if customers pay late.
Fixed costs (rent, salaries, loan installments) must be paid no matter what. Variable costs (ingredients, packaging) grow and shrink with sales.
Keep business and personal money in separate accounts. Pay yourself a planned amount from the business instead of dipping into the company account whenever you need cash.
A budget is a plan made before the month starts: money in, money out, and what is left.

title: Emergency fund
subtitle: Your shield against the unexpected
topics: Build a safety buffer on top of good cash flow: how many months of costs are worth securing.
How the size of the fund differs for an employee, a freelancer and a business with unpredictable costs (e.g. food service or manufacturing).
Where to keep the fund so it is safe and quick to reach.
challenge: Put aside the first part of your emergency fund while paying your current bills and a sudden small cost.

lessonCard.title: A cushion for bad days
points: An emergency fund is cash set aside only for surprises: a broken fridge, a client who pays late, a sudden repair.
A common rule of thumb is 3–6 months of essential costs. A business with unpredictable costs or income, like a restaurant, needs a bigger cushion than someone with a steady salary.
Keep it safe and easy to reach, e.g. in a separate savings account, not in stocks or a long-term deposit.
Build it step by step: a small fixed amount every month adds up.

title: Insurance and risk
subtitle: Protection against big losses
topics: Move from saving for small crises to protecting yourself against big losses that an emergency fund alone cannot cover.
Personal insurance (health, life, loss of income) and business insurance (liability, property, equipment and machinery).
How to read exclusions, deductibles and sums insured.
challenge: Choose insurance that fits your life and your business. Disaster may strike before you are covered, so learn from it.

lessonCard.title: Insure what you can't afford to lose
points: An emergency fund covers small shocks. Insurance is for big losses the fund cannot cover: a fire, a serious illness, a lawsuit.
Personal: health, life and loss-of-income insurance. Business: liability, property and equipment insurance.
Always check the exclusions (what is NOT covered), the deductible (the part you pay yourself) and the sum insured (the maximum payout).
Insurance only helps if you have it before something happens.

title: Taxes
subtitle: Costs you don't see right away
topics: With cash flow, a buffer and risk under control, it is time for mandatory public charges.
Basics of income tax, VAT and social contributions, in personal life and in business.
How taxes affect real profit, product prices and cash planning for the coming months.
challenge: Set aside cash for the tax deadline without touching your emergency fund.

title: Personal and business debt
subtitle: When a loan helps and when it hurts
topics: What to do when current funds are not enough.
"Good" debt (investing in growth or assets) vs. "bad" debt (paying for everyday spending or covering losses).
The cost of money over time: interest, APR, fees and the repayment schedule.
challenge: Compare two loan offers and pay an installment on a tight budget.

title: Debt financing
subtitle: Loans, bonds and installments in business
topics: Using debt as part of a growth strategy in the middle of the year.
Bank loan, leasing, overdraft or a bond issue: matching the instrument to the goal and the industry.
How debt affects stability when sales drop or interest rates rise.
challenge: Finance new equipment or an expansion with debt while keeping safe liquidity.

title: Legal forms of business
subtitle: Liability and taxes
topics: How the legal structure of a business protects your assets.
The main forms: sole proprietorship, civil partnership, limited liability company, joint-stock company, limited partnership.
Owners' liability, bringing in investors and the tax consequences of each form.
challenge: Choose or change your company's legal form as risk and capital needs grow.

title: Stocks and bonds
subtitle: Putting surplus money to work
topics: Investing surplus capital once the budget, debt and legal form are in order.
Stocks (a share in a company's ownership and growth) and bonds (lending money to the issuer).
Risk, liquidity, time horizon and diversification in personal and business portfolios.
challenge: Build a diversified portfolio with the capital you have and react to market swings.

title: Financial leverage
subtitle: Multiplying profit and risk
topics: Debt and financial assets combined in one mechanism.
Financial and operating leverage: how borrowed money or fixed costs boost returns in good times.
The dark side: the same mechanism speeds up losses in a downturn.
challenge: Use leverage in an investment or a business project and survive a market correction.

title: Dividends
subtitle: Pay yourself or reinvest?
topics: Where dividends come from and when a company may pay them.
Why not every profitable company pays a dividend.
The dilemma: pay the profit to yourself or keep it in the company for growth (R&D, expansion).
challenge: Decide how to split your company's profit between your own needs and competing on the market.

title: Pre-emptive rights
subtitle: Defending your stake and raising capital
topics: Raising capital for the next cycle before the end of the year.
Pre-emptive rights and rights of first refusal: subscribing to new shares and contract clauses when shares are sold.
How a new share issue or a share sale dilutes your stake and your control.
challenge: Decide whether to use your pre-emptive right, sell it, or let your stake be diluted.

title: Annual review and strategy
subtitle: Closing the year
topics: Summing up all 12 months and connecting personal and business finances.
Net worth (assets minus debts), emergency fund, insurance coverage and tax efficiency.
Learning from the year's mistakes and successes.
